days.title: Matching Agent Failures to Context Techniques and the Databricks Stack

concepts.heading: From failure symptom to technique
concepts.body: Context engineering means deciding what enters the model's window, in what form and when. Most of its vocabulary (attention budget, compaction, trimming, tool result scoping, sub-agent) is the exam guide's terminology or generally accepted practice. Databricks documents the tooling around it, not these techniques as features. The exam asks you to match a symptom to the technique that addresses it most directly. A long history of old tool outputs that makes the agent ignore the latest constraint calls for compaction: older turns become a short note of decisions, constraints, open tasks and identifiers, while recent turns stay verbatim. Trimming only drops the oldest messages, so a constraint stated early disappears. A tool that returns thousands of rows calls for scoping at the source: filter parameters, a row limit and only the needed columns, rather than asking the model to ignore the excess. Noisy, high-volume side work belongs in a sub-agent that returns a compact result. Two contradicting instructions need one rewritten rule with explicit precedence, because more text does not resolve a conflict.

concepts.heading: Proactive strategies before compaction
concepts.body: Compaction is a late, lossy step, so the exam rewards designs that keep pressure low earlier. These strategies are generally accepted practice rather than Databricks features, but Databricks tooling supports each of them. Minimal tool sets: every tool definition costs tokens on every call and invites wrong choices, so give the agent only the tools the task needs. The MCP governance documentation lets you restrict which tools of a server are exposed. Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references in context, such as table names or document identifiers, and load the full item with a tool only when the step needs it. This suits a corpus too large to preload. Tool result scoping: shape what a tool returns before it reaches the window. Relevant memory only: retrieve the memories that matter for the current request instead of injecting the whole store. Tool descriptions: say when a retriever tool should be used, so unneeded calls do not add text. When a scenario asks what reduces pressure before compaction becomes necessary, pick the option that prevents the tokens from entering.

concepts.heading: Four failure modes in a trace
concepts.body: The exam names four context failure modes. They are the exam guide's terms, not Databricks product features, so learn the symptom of each. Context poisoning: one wrong value enters the context and keeps being cited as fact. If that value is written to durable memory, it poisons every later conversation, so you fix the stored entry and validate what the pipeline writes. Context distraction: a long, accurate history makes the agent repeat past actions or ignore the current goal. Compact it or move finished work out of the window. Context confusion: look-alike or unnecessary tool definitions misdirect the choice of tool. Trim the tool set and differentiate the descriptions. Context clash: retrieved sources or instructions contradict each other inside one context. Retrieve only the authoritative version or give a precedence rule. To tell poisoning from clash, count the sources: poisoning is one false item trusted repeatedly, clash is two items that disagree. In an MLflow trace, read the span inputs to see which text the agent actually received before it acted.

concepts.heading: Choosing the right Databricks tool
concepts.body: Scenario questions ask which product holds a piece of the solution. Unity Catalog governs access: privileges on tables, volumes and functions, plus the comments that describe them. Sharing a custom tool across agents means registering it as a Unity Catalog function and controlling who may call it with EXECUTE. Lakebase backs the managed stores for state: agent sessions hold the state of one interaction, and agent memory holds durable facts recalled in later conversations, scoped to a subject. State that must outlive a process or a conversation belongs there. MCP exposes tools to the agent. Databricks recommends the Genie One MCP server (generally available) for natural-language analytics across the workspace, while a Genie Agent MCP answers questions scoped to one curated Genie Agent. Unity Gateway grants and policies govern the Databricks-provided MCP servers; Genie Agent MCP calls bypass it and rely on permissions on the Genie Agent and its data. MLflow 3 Tracing records inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every step, so it answers questions about what happened in a run.

examPoints: Match the symptom to the technique first, then check that the fix does not drop information the agent still needs.
Context poisoning is one wrong value cited repeatedly, distraction is a long accurate history, confusion is look-alike tools, clash is contradicting sources.
Sessions and memory are Lakebase-backed, EXECUTE governs shared functions, MLflow Tracing shows per-step tokens and latency.

quiz.q: An agent calls a tool that returns every column of thousands of order rows. The trace shows the next model call is dominated by this output, and answers get worse. Which change addresses this most directly?
choices: Raise the model's temperature so the agent varies how it reads the large tool output
Compact the whole conversation into one summary after every tool call so earlier output never accumulates
Scope the result at the source with filter parameters, a row limit and only the needed columns
Move to a model with a larger context window and leave the tool output exactly as it is
quiz.explain: Scoping at the source keeps the extra rows from ever entering the window. Compacting after every call is lossy and treats the symptom late. A larger window delays the limit without removing the noise, and temperature has no link to what the prompt contains.

quiz.q: An agent retrieves two policy documents that state different return windows, and its answers switch between them. Which failure mode is this, and what is the fix?
choices: Context clash; retrieve only the authoritative version or give an explicit precedence rule
Context poisoning; delete the agent's session store so the stale document is forgotten for good
Context confusion; reduce the number of registered tools so the agent stops mixing documents
Context distraction; compact the long history so the agent stops repeating earlier answers
quiz.explain: Two sources that disagree inside one context are a clash. Poisoning is a single false item trusted repeatedly, confusion is about tool choice, and distraction is about a long accurate history. These are the exam guide's terms, not Databricks features.

days.recap: Pick the technique by symptom: compaction for crowded history, source-side scoping for noisy tool output, sub-agents for noisy side work, precedence rules for clashes. Prevent pressure first with minimal tools and just-in-time retrieval. Know which product does what: Unity Catalog governs, Lakebase stores sessions and memory, MCP exposes tools, MLflow Tracing shows each step.

days.title: Attention Budget, Reasoning Modes and Long-Context Degradation

concepts.heading: Finding what eats the attention budget
concepts.body: Attention budget is the exam guide's term for the idea that a model's focus is limited even when the window is not full. Too much low-value text dilutes the part that matters. Databricks documentation gives a parallel for Genie: too many instructions can reduce effectiveness, especially in longer conversations, because Genie might struggle to prioritize the most important guidance. The method is to measure, then cut the largest contributor. MLflow Tracing records inputs, outputs and token usage for every step, so you can find the span that adds the most tokens. Then change that element at its source; these remedies are generally accepted practice, not Databricks features. Stale history is compacted. Large tool results are scoped. Many near-identical few-shot examples are replaced by a few diverse ones. An always-on prompt is limited to rules that apply to every request, with situational guidance loaded on demand. Duplicate retrieved passages are removed before they enter the context, because repeated text costs budget and distorts weight. The wrong answers on the exam usually add capacity, such as a bigger window, or remove something at random.

concepts.heading: Choosing the reasoning mode
concepts.body: Standard, extended thinking and reduced thinking are the exam's names for three modes. Databricks documents how reasoning behaves: reasoning models produce reasoning tokens in addition to normal input and output tokens, and higher reasoning effort can improve accuracy on complex tasks at the cost of more latency and token usage. So the decision is a trade-off, justified by evidence. Use extended thinking where an evaluation shows it improves accuracy on hard, constrained problems and latency and cost allow it. Use standard or reduced thinking for simple lookups, routing or formatting steps where it adds cost without gain. Do not buy reasoning tokens to compensate for noisy input; reduce the context instead. You can also decide per step: think hard only where the task is hard. Model-specific details change, so stay with the stem. For example, the docs state that some newer Claude models reject a manual budget_tokens value and use adaptive thinking with an effort setting instead.

concepts.heading: Thinking tokens and the window
concepts.body: The reasoning mode also changes how many tokens the window and the output allowance must carry. For models that accept a manual thinking budget, the Databricks documentation states that budget_tokens must be less than max_tokens. Reasoning that consumes the whole allowance would leave no room for the visible answer, so plan the output limit as thinking plus answer. In multi-turn conversations with databricks-claude-sonnet-4-5, only the reasoning blocks of the last assistant turn or tool-use session are visible to the model and counted as input tokens. If the model does not need to reason over its earlier thinking, you can omit the reasoning block when resending history. On the exam, questions in this area give you a latency target, a token budget and an evaluation result. Choose the cheapest mode that meets the accuracy requirement, and reject answers that raise the thinking budget while the real problem is an oversized prompt.

concepts.heading: Where length degrades quality
concepts.body: Long context can degrade retrieval accuracy or reasoning quality well before the window is full. The window size is a ceiling, not a target. Detecting the point is an evidence question: evaluate the agent on tasks at different context sizes, for example with mlflow.genai.evaluate(), and read token counts from traces. A quality drop that tracks context size, not task difficulty, shows degradation. The interventions are generally accepted practice rather than Databricks features, and all of them send less. Retrieve with a focused query instead of the whole transcript. Keep the retrieved set small and well ranked, since more text is not better context. Place the key text near the question. Split a long reading task into small extraction steps and reason over the extracts. Compact history that is no longer needed. Set a context budget from measured accuracy against token count, not from the advertised window. Adding capacity only moves the cliff.

examPoints: Use the trace to find the largest token contributor and shrink it at the source; more window capacity does not restore focus.
Choose extended thinking only where evaluation shows a gain; budget_tokens must be below max_tokens, and some newer Claude models use adaptive thinking instead.
Degradation is shown by accuracy falling as context grows; the fix sends less, ranked and focused, and sets the budget from measurements.

quiz.q: A routing step in an agent only labels each request as billing or technical. An evaluation shows extended thinking gives no accuracy gain on this step, and users complain about latency. Which choice fits the exam's reasoning guidance?
choices: Keep extended thinking on for every step, because more reasoning can never lower the quality of any answer
Use a larger thinking budget on this step so the labels become more stable across repeated runs of the evaluation
Move the routing instructions to the end of a longer prompt so the model has more material to reason over
Use standard or reduced thinking for this step and keep extended thinking for the hard steps only
quiz.explain: Reasoning costs latency and tokens, and the evaluation shows no gain here, so the cheaper mode is justified for this step. Keeping the expensive mode where it helps is the per-step decision. A bigger budget or a longer prompt adds cost without evidence of benefit.

quiz.q: An agent answers correctly with about a quarter of its window used, but accuracy drops sharply once retrieved text grows past a measured size. Which intervention most directly restores performance?
choices: Switch to a model with a larger advertised window so the same retrieved text fits comfortably as is
Retrieve a smaller ranked set with a focused query and set the budget from the accuracy curve
Append the full conversation transcript to every retrieval query so the retriever has maximum information
Raise max_tokens so the answer has more room after the longer retrieved text has been read
quiz.explain: The measurements show quality falls with context size, so sending less and better ranked text addresses the cause. A larger window moves the ceiling but not the degradation point. Sending the whole transcript to the retriever adds noise, and max_tokens only affects output.

days.recap: Cut the largest contributor found in the trace. Spend thinking tokens only where evaluation shows a gain, and keep budget_tokens under max_tokens. Judge degradation by accuracy against context size, and fix it by sending less, ranked and focused, never by adding window.

days.title: Genie Instructions, Few-Shot Examples and Prompt Cost

concepts.heading: Layering a production-ready Genie space
concepts.body: Databricks calls Genie spaces Genie Agents, and the exam guide uses the older name. The curation guidance is a layering rule. Column descriptions in Unity Catalog come first. SQL expressions define business semantics such as metrics and filters. Example SQL queries, static or parameterized, teach Genie to handle complex or ambiguous questions. Text instructions are a last resort for guidance that SQL cannot express, such as rounding rules. Keep all instruction types consistent: if text says to round to two digits, the example queries must round too. Write specific instructions. A clarification rule names a trigger, the missing details, the required action to ask first, and example wording, and it goes at the end of the general instructions. Parameterized example queries and SQL functions are trusted assets that give verified answers. Sample questions configured in the agent settings appear in the chat window to help users start exploring; example queries are what teach Genie. Before release, score accuracy with benchmark questions and review the generated SQL. Start small and add context based on feedback. For misread domain vocabulary, the exam's sample answer defines the terms in general instructions.

concepts.heading: Few-shot examples under a token budget
concepts.body: Every few-shot example spends attention budget on every call, so the exam asks you to justify each one by its marginal contribution. This is generally accepted practice, not a Databricks feature. Include an example when it covers a tool path the evaluation never exercises, demonstrates the required output structure, or shows how to handle an ambiguous input, since these are the cases where the model most needs a pattern. Exclude near-copies of an example you already have, easy cases the model already handles, and examples whose incidental details the model would copy. Vary the details across examples so the model copies the structure, not the facts. Decide from measured score changes and token cost, not from opinion or length: keep the smallest set that captures the gain, and drop an example whose removal does not lower the score. If the candidate set exceeds the budget, a common alternative is to retrieve the few most relevant examples for each request instead of including all of them.

concepts.heading: Targeted prompt revision
concepts.body: A miscalibrated system prompt shows a failure pattern, and the best revision is the smallest one that removes it. The principle follows the same logic as Genie's guidance to write clear, specific instructions and avoid vague ones. A narrow failure, such as the wrong argument format in one tool, needs a short specific rule or a precise error message returned by the tool, not a rewrite. A vague rule is made specific with a concrete example, not with emphasis or extra bulk. When you retest a Genie change, use a new chat, because earlier turns can influence its responses. After several patches, consolidate the prompt into one coherent version and re-run the same evaluation to check for regressions. When only some requests need a rule, keep the shared prompt stable and inject the variable rules per request (generally accepted practice), so the cost is not paid by everyone. Rewriting the whole prompt, adding a large block of examples or switching to extended reasoning all raise token cost and maintenance burden for a narrow problem.

concepts.heading: Is the higher-token prompt worth it?
concepts.body: Experiment tracking turns this into a measurement. Databricks documents mlflow.genai.evaluate(), which scores a whole app version on an evaluation dataset so that versions can be compared. A comparison is valid only when the dataset and scorers are identical in both runs; otherwise a score change cannot be attributed to the prompt. Judge the larger prompt by its effect on the slice of questions it targets and by the absence of regressions elsewhere, then weigh the gain against token cost. Because the system prompt is paid on every call, multiply the added tokens by the number of model calls per task, and confirm with per-span token usage from MLflow Tracing. To identify which prompt element drives the trade-off, change one element at a time and rerun, a generally accepted ablation practice. Keep the bigger prompt when valid score deltas show a targeted gain, no regressions and token usage inside the budget. Reject it when the gain is within noise or the datasets differ.

examPoints: Layer Genie context: column descriptions, SQL expressions, example SQL and trusted assets first, text instructions last, all consistent.
Keep a few-shot example only if it covers an untested path, shows the output structure or handles ambiguity, and its measured gain justifies its tokens.
Compare prompts on the same dataset and scorers; multiply added tokens by calls per task and check the targeted slice for gain and regressions.

quiz.q: Genie Agent users define the metric active customers in three different ways in text instructions, and the generated SQL varies. Which change is the most reliable fix?
choices: Define the metric once as a SQL expression and make any example queries use the same definition
Add a longer text instruction in capital letters that forbids every definition except one of the three
Remove all example queries so only the text instructions can influence how the metric is computed
Add the three definitions as sample questions so users see each version of the metric listed in chat
quiz.explain: SQL expressions are the structured place for metrics and filters, and consistent definitions across instruction types avoid conflicts. Text is a last resort, removing examples loses verified patterns, and sample questions only seed the chat rather than define logic.

quiz.q: An agent calls one tool with dates in the wrong format. The evaluation shows every other behavior is correct. Which revision resolves it at the least token and maintenance cost?
choices: Rewrite the whole system prompt into a new structure and include twenty new few-shot examples of tool calls
Switch the agent to extended thinking so the model reasons about each argument before it calls the tool
Add one specific rule with a correct date example, or return a precise error message from the tool
Move the full tool documentation into the system prompt so it is available on every call of the agent
quiz.explain: A narrow failure needs a narrow fix, and a short rule with an example costs few tokens. A full rewrite, many examples, extended reasoning or bulk documentation raise cost on every call for a one-tool problem.

days.recap: Genie context goes in layers (descriptions, SQL expressions, example SQL, trusted assets) with text last and no conflicts. Justify few-shot examples by marginal gain per token. Fix narrow failures with narrow rules, and approve a bigger prompt only on same-dataset, same-scorer evidence that its gain beats its per-call cost.

days.title: Metadata, Curated Objects and AI Search Diagnosis

concepts.heading: Metadata gaps behind an accuracy problem
concepts.body: Genie reads Unity Catalog table and column names and descriptions to generate SQL, and the documentation calls quality descriptions critical for accuracy. So when an agent returns wrong results, look for ambiguous column names with no comment, coded values with no documented meaning, and business terms defined nowhere. The highest-impact fix is usually a precise column comment on the columns the failing questions use, because it is cheap, durable and shared by every consumer. AI-generated comments are a starting point: they describe an object from its schema, the documentation states they must be reviewed, and ambiguous ones should be replaced with the real business definition. Genie also allows agent-level descriptions and synonyms. These are scoped to that agent and do not overwrite Unity Catalog metadata, so put shared meaning in Unity Catalog and agent-specific interpretation in Genie. For coded columns, document what each code means and define business terms as SQL expressions. Entity matching supplies representative values such as mapping FL to Florida, not the meaning of a code.

concepts.heading: Curating objects into a Genie space
concepts.body: Curation means attaching the governed objects Genie should use, and instructions cannot bring an unattached object into context. Databricks advises keeping the agent focused on a defined topic and audience and including only tables needed for its questions. Views and metric views help because they pre-join tables and pre-define metrics, dimensions and aggregations. Hide confusing or unimportant columns. For logic too complex for a single query, register a SQL function in Unity Catalog as a trusted asset. Genie can call scalar and table-valued functions with user-supplied parameters and cannot view or modify the SQL inside, which suits sealed logic. Users need EXECUTE on the function. For recurring questions that differ only in values, use a parameterized example query, giving each parameter a comment that describes its allowed values. Leave out duplicates, superseded tables and unrelated tables, and mark old tables deprecated in Unity Catalog. When the exam asks what to add, prefer a few governed, pre-joined objects over many raw ones.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing AI Search retrieval problems
concepts.body: Databricks AI Search supports approximate nearest neighbor, hybrid and full-text query types. Hybrid combines semantic and keyword results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion and is the recommended starting point; it fixes queries with exact identifiers such as product codes that pure semantic similarity ranks poorly. Full-text search is Beta, so it is never the answer. When the correct chunk is retrieved but ranked low, add the reranker, which re-scores results, and keep the final result count small instead of returning more chunks. Filters sharpen precision: a key with no operator is an exact match, and comparisons put the operator in the key, such as a key ending in a less-than sign. A wrong filter key is a common root cause of missing results. If only the first query after an idle period fails, check whether the embedding endpoint scales to zero; the documentation recommends removing that default because a cold endpoint can time out the first query. Match the remedy to the symptom: signal quality improves with ranking and filters, not with more or bigger chunks.

examPoints: Fix the metadata gap first: precise Unity Catalog column comments, reviewed AI drafts, and documented meanings for coded columns.
Curate few governed, pre-joined objects; use SQL functions and parameterized queries as trusted assets, and remove duplicates.
Match the AI Search remedy to the symptom: hybrid for exact identifiers, reranker for poor ranking, filters for precision, no scale to zero for cold-start failures.

quiz.q: A Genie Agent computes revenue from the wrong column. The table has amt_gross and amt_net with no comments, and both appear in the failing questions. Which change has the highest impact?
choices: Add a long text instruction in the agent that lists every column name of the table in alphabetical order
Add precise Unity Catalog column comments that state what each amount column includes and when to use it
Turn on entity matching for both amount columns so Genie can sample representative numeric values from them
Add more sample questions to the agent so that users see the revenue question displayed in the chat
quiz.explain: Column descriptions in Unity Catalog are the cheapest, most durable context for choosing the right column. Entity matching supplies example values, not meaning, and sample questions only help users start exploring. A column list in text instructions adds tokens without meaning.

quiz.q: An agent searches a product index. Queries that contain exact SKU codes often miss the right chunk, while descriptive queries work well. Which remediation most directly improves the signal quality?
choices: Double the chunk size so each SKU appears inside a larger block of surrounding text in the whole index
Increase num_results so that more candidate chunks reach the agent for each of the SKU queries
Switch to the Beta full-text search so keyword matching replaces vector similarity for every query type
Use hybrid search so keyword matching complements semantic similarity, with a reranker for order
quiz.explain: Exact identifiers are matched by keywords, and hybrid retrieval combines them with semantic similarity. Larger chunks and more results add noise rather than precision, and full-text search is Beta and would hurt the descriptive queries.

days.recap: Fix meaning before logic: precise reviewed Unity Catalog comments beat extra text instructions. Curate a few governed, pre-joined objects and use SQL functions or parameterized queries as trusted assets. For AI Search, read the symptom: hybrid for identifiers, reranker for ranking, filters for precision, and no scale to zero on the embedding endpoint.

days.title: RAG over Governed Documents, Chunking and Task Context

concepts.heading: A RAG pipeline over governed documents
concepts.body: Databricks describes the pipeline for unstructured data in stages: corpus composition and ingestion, parsing, enrichment (metadata extraction, deduplication, filtering), chunking, embedding, and indexing. Keep the raw source stored for traceability. Documents live in a Unity Catalog volume, so the agent identity needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and READ VOLUME, and no more. Chunks and metadata sit in a Delta table that backs a Delta Sync AI Search index, which stays synced as the source updates and enables filtering on metadata stored beside the embeddings. Keep metadata such as source and section so answers can cite. At retrieval, the agent calls a retriever tool, the best chunks are appended to the query, and only the columns the agent needs are returned while the rest serve for filtering. Deduplicate before indexing, because duplicates create redundant chunks that hurt performance. As generally accepted practice, replace a reprocessed file's old chunks instead of appending, so stale versions do not clash, and for a few short documents read whole, direct read tools can be simpler than an index.

concepts.heading: Selecting a chunking strategy
concepts.body: Databricks lists four strategies: fixed-size, paragraph-based, format-specific and semantic. Fixed-size is quick but rarely gives semantically coherent chunks and is described as rarely suitable for production. Format-specific chunking uses inherent structure, such as Markdown headers or HTML sections, to define boundaries. The documentation states there is no one-size-fits-all choice, so decide from three inputs. Document structure: cut where the document's own structure ends a unit, for example a definition, and keep the parent heading as metadata. Embedding model limits: know the model's maximum input in tokens, because text beyond it is truncated and information is lost, and count everything sent into the embedding call. Query types: lookups of a specific answer suit small precise sections, while a question about a whole document may need a larger or summary unit (generally accepted practice). Overlap between chunks preserves continuity. Size chunks to the span where answers actually sit, and avoid chunks so large that irrelevant text dilutes the retrieved context.

concepts.heading: Scoping the context an agent needs
concepts.body: Select the context elements for a task from what the agent must do, not from what is available. The element list is generally accepted practice and the exam's framing, not a Databricks feature. A well-scoped task usually needs: the instruction and its constraints, the one record or document the action applies to, who is asking, runtime state such as the current date and time zone, the schemas of the tools it may call, the shape of the finished output, and a statement of what the agent covers and where to send the rest. Each unneeded element spends attention budget and invites distraction, so exclude speculative data and unrelated tables. This mirrors the Databricks advice that a Genie Agent should answer questions for a particular topic and audience, not across various domains. Runtime context resolves relative phrases: without the date and time zone, last week has no meaning. Pass the identity so permissions and personalization apply. When two options both seem useful, choose the one the task needs to execute correctly.

examPoints: Governed RAG: volume privileges, chunks and metadata in a Delta table behind an AI Search index, minimal returned columns, replace stale chunks.
Choose chunking from document structure, the embedding model's maximum input and the query types; keep the parent heading as metadata.
Scope context to the task: instruction, the one record, identity, runtime state, tool schemas, output shape and scope; nothing speculative.

quiz.q: An agent answers questions about policy definitions. Each definition is a short subsection under a numbered heading, and answers always sit inside one subsection. Which chunking design fits best?
choices: Fixed windows of the embedding model's full maximum input, split without regard to headings
One chunk per entire document so every answer is surrounded by the complete policy text
Chunk at subsection boundaries and store the parent heading as metadata beside each chunk
Chunk every sentence separately and drop the headings so that retrieval stays as small as it can be
quiz.explain: Cutting where the document's own structure ends a unit keeps each answer whole, and the heading metadata keeps the context. Fixed windows split definitions, whole documents dilute the context, and sentence chunks lose the surrounding definition.

quiz.q: An agent must read PDFs from a Unity Catalog volume for retrieval and nothing else. Which grant set follows least privilege?
choices: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents plus READ VOLUME on the volume
ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog that holds the volume, so later schema changes never block the agent
WRITE VOLUME on the volume plus MODIFY on the schema, so the agent can fix parsing problems itself
READ VOLUME on the volume alone, since the parent catalog and schema do not need any grants
quiz.explain: Reading a volume requires USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents and READ VOLUME on the volume. ALL PRIVILEGES and write access exceed what retrieval needs, and READ VOLUME alone is not enough without the parent privileges.

days.recap: Governed RAG means minimal volume grants, a Delta table of chunks plus metadata behind an AI Search index, returning only needed columns, and replacing stale chunks. Chunk by document structure within the embedding model's input limit and the query types. Scope each task's context to the elements it needs to execute, no more.

days.title: Retrieval Timing, Failure Diagnosis and Authoritative Sources

concepts.heading: Pre-inference versus just-in-time retrieval
concepts.body: Retrieval can run at two moments, and the exam asks you to pick one for a use case. Pre-inference retrieval means the application queries the index before the model call and places the chunks in the prompt. It always happens, costs one model call and gives predictable latency. Just-in-time (JIT) agentic retrieval means the agent holds a retriever tool and decides during its run whether, when and what to search. Be precise about the source of these names: the Databricks docs describe the mechanisms but do not define the two terms, so they are the exam guide's vocabulary and generally accepted practice. The documented mechanism for JIT is a retriever tool such as VectorSearchRetrieverTool from AI Bridge, which exposes an AI Search index as a tool, with a description that tells the agent when to search. Pick pre-inference when every request needs the same source and grounding is mandatory. Pick JIT when the next lookup depends on what the last one found, as with a coding agent exploring files. JIT costs extra model round trips and relies on the model choosing to search.

concepts.heading: Deciding per context element, not per agent
concepts.body: The choice is made for each context element, so one agent can use both timings. Facts that are always needed, small and fetched by a known key, such as a caller's plan, contract date and open case, are cheap and certain to be required. Load them before inference and skip a model round trip. Knowledge whose need depends on how the conversation unfolds, such as which article fits a diagnosis the agent has not reached yet, belongs behind a retriever tool. Loading those articles up front would usually fetch irrelevant text, because the first message rarely reveals the diagnosis, and irrelevant text dilutes the facts that matter. Two traps appear on the exam. Putting a mandatory behavior behind a tool is one: a stronger prompt only lowers the chance of skipping, so if citations are required on every answer, retrieve in application code before inference. That also puts a RETRIEVER span in every traced run, so retrieval judges can score every run. The other trap is loading everything into the prompt, which spends the attention budget on text that is mostly irrelevant.

concepts.heading: Reading a retrieval failure from eval logs
concepts.body: When answers are wrong, read the judge scores together with the retrieval spans. MLflow 3 built-in judges score retrieval separately. RetrievalRelevance asks whether the retrieved context is relevant to the request. RetrievalGroundedness asks whether the response is grounded in that context. RetrievalSufficiency asks whether the context contains what the ground-truth expectations need, so it requires expectations, as does Correctness. A retrieval span is a RETRIEVER span whose output is a list of documents, which makes the retrieved content inspectable. The failure names below are the exam's convention, not a Databricks taxonomy. High relevance with low sufficiency means on-topic text that lacks the needed content: the authoritative source is probably not in the corpus, and Unity Catalog metadata showing what feeds the index confirms it. Sufficient but ungrounded points at the prompt or model. Chunk size, a reranker or a larger candidate pool cannot supply text that is absent, so the governance action is to onboard the missing source to the indexed corpus.

concepts.heading: Constraining retrieval to authoritative sources
concepts.body: Unity Catalog lets stewards flag assets with the system.certification_status tag, whose values are certified and deprecated. Setting it needs ASSIGN on that governed tag, plus ownership of the object or APPLY TAG, USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG. The docs describe the tag as a signal of trust or lifecycle. They do not say it blocks queries, so a certified label alone does not stop an agent from reading an uncertified staging table. Enforcement comes from what the retriever is built on and from grants. A pre-deployment strategy, which is a practice rather than a documented procedure, has three steps: curate approved documents in one governed location, certify them and deprecate superseded copies, then build the AI Search index only from that source and grant the agent's service principal only what it needs. Databricks recommends least privilege and a dedicated service principal per app, so a permission error on an unapproved source is the control working. As a practice, limit ASSIGN on the tag to stewards so teams cannot certify their own copies, and separate corpora by audience. Check evaluation-trace documents before release. Prompt rules are not access controls.

examPoints: Pre-inference versus JIT retrieval are the exam's terms, not Databricks-defined: choose pre-inference when every request needs the source and grounding is mandatory, JIT when the next lookup depends on the previous result.

Read judge scores with retrieval spans: high RetrievalRelevance with low RetrievalSufficiency and a source missing from the index means onboard the authoritative asset; chunking or reranking cannot add absent text.
The certification tag is a label, not enforcement: constrain retrieval by curating and certifying, building the index from the approved source and scoping the service principal's grants.

quiz.q: A refund-policy chatbot must ground every answer in one policy index, and the team wants one model call per question with predictable latency. Which design fits?
choices: Give the agent a retriever tool and instruct it in the system prompt to always search before answering
Query the index in application code before the model call and place the top chunks in the prompt
Let the agent answer first, then run a second call that retrieves evidence and corrects the answer
Place the complete policy library in the system prompt so no retrieval step is needed at all
quiz.explain: The application queries the index on every request, so retrieval always happens and one model call is enough. A prompt instruction only lowers the chance of skipping, a post-answer pass adds a call and lets ungrounded text escape, and the full library wastes attention budget.

quiz.q: An agent's service principal holds SELECT on a whole catalog. The steward certified the approved tables, yet a trace shows the agent returning rows from an uncertified staging table. What is the right conclusion and fix?
choices: The tag is only a label and does not block reads, so scope the grants and retrieval source to certified assets
Certification changes are slow to take effect, so wait for the tag to propagate across the metastore before testing again
Certification should be reapplied to the staging table so the agent will treat it as the approved source from now on
Certification can be enforced by naming the tag in the system prompt and telling the agent to obey it strictly
quiz.explain: The tag signals trust but does not stop queries; the broad SELECT still permits staging reads. Limiting grants and building the retriever from certified assets creates the boundary. Waiting, tagging the staging table or naming the tag in a prompt enforces nothing.

days.recap: Pick pre-inference retrieval when grounding is mandatory and the source is fixed, JIT when needs are unpredictable. Diagnose with judges and retrieval spans, fix missing sources in the corpus, and enforce authority with certification plus scoped grants.

days.title: Memory Types, Delta-Backed State and Retrieving Memories

concepts.heading: Matching the memory type to the information need
concepts.body: Databricks documents two managed stores, both backed by Lakebase and usable from agents built on any framework. Agent sessions hold the state of one interaction, most commonly the ordered transcript of messages, tool calls and results, but also any state a framework persists, such as a LangGraph graph. Agent memory holds durable facts, preferences and decisions that the agent recalls in later, separate conversations, retrieved by semantic search. A session is scoped to one interaction; a memory is scoped to a subject, such as a user. The docs say to use both together for most cases, sessions alone for in-interaction state, and memory alone when the framework already manages session state. Diagnose a mismatch with one test: must the information still be available after this conversation ends and a different one begins? If yes, it needs memory. If it only matters while the chat continues, the session already covers it, and a window that fills during one long task is a within-conversation problem for trimming or compaction, not for adding long-term memory. Short-term versus long-term memory is general agent vocabulary.

concepts.heading: Episodic and derived memory
concepts.body: The stateful-agents page says Databricks memory research describes the same architecture with different terms. The session store holds episodic memory, the raw record of each session. The memory store holds derived memory, the facts and workflows distilled from those sessions. A memory pipeline is the offline process, called the dreaming process, that reads sessions, extracts durable facts, writes them to the memory store and consolidates them over time, on demand or on a schedule. This matters for context because recalled memory enters the window. Raw episodic records spend attention budget on greetings and repeated text, while distilled facts carry the signal in few tokens. The layers also serve different needs: a compliance team wanting a complete, replayable record reads sessions, while personalization reads memory. The stores are independent, so deleting a session, or an entire session store, does not delete memories already retained in the memory store. Removing a memory therefore means acting on the memory store itself.

concepts.heading: Delta-backed state object versus in-context scratchpad
concepts.body: A scratchpad is working notes kept inside the context window, such as a plan or a running list. It is a generally accepted agent term, not a Databricks-documented feature, and the exam uses it for state that lives only in context. It is cheap and has no read or write latency, so it is enough when state is needed only until the turn or task ends, losing it costs a retry rather than wrong side effects, and it is small. It fails for long or shared work. Notes disappear with the window on a restart, can be summarized away by compaction, cost attention on every turn, and can pile up stale entries that distract the model. Delta-backed state object is the exam's term for a plain Delta table in Unity Catalog, with no Preview feature involved. It is durable, queryable with SQL and shared by every run or agent. Use it for multi-day workflows, parallel agents that must see each other's progress, auditable records, and exact counters or positions. The agent reads only the row it needs and writes status back.

concepts.heading: Structured query or AI Search over stored memories
concepts.body: Lakebase is managed Postgres, so ordinary SQL, keys and indexes apply to records you keep in your own tables there. A structured query returns exact values deterministically when the agent knows the key and the field, such as a customer's current plan tier, a count over a date range or a record with a known identifier. Semantic search, through Databricks AI Search or the semantic recall of agent memory, ranks by similarity of meaning and suits free-text recall where the user paraphrases, because an embedding can match a note about anxiety to a question about stress. Equality and LIKE filters fail on paraphrase. Identifiers such as SKUs carry little semantic signal, and the docs say AI Search hybrid keyword-similarity search, which merges vector and keyword results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, helps where data has unique keywords. Ownership is a predicate, not a similarity: scope a shared store with a metadata filter on the query or a WHERE clause so other customers' rows never become candidates. A prompt or score threshold is not that control.

examPoints: Sessions are scoped to one interaction, memory to a subject; use memory only when information must survive into a separate conversation, and fix a filling window with trimming or compaction.
Use a Delta-backed state object (a plain Unity Catalog table) when state must survive restarts, be shared across agents, be audited or stay exact; a scratchpad suffices for small, short-lived state.
Structured SQL for known keys, columns and aggregates; semantic search for paraphrased free text; hybrid search for identifiers inside prose; a filter, not a prompt, for tenant scope.

quiz.q: A travel agent's framework checkpointer already persists each chat so it resumes after a restart. Travelers complain that a seat preference stated in one chat is unknown in a later chat. What is the mismatch?
choices: The session store is too small, so the transcript should be extended to hold many more past chats at once
The context window is too short, so older turns of the current chat must be summarized and trimmed
There is in-interaction state but no durable, subject-scoped memory to carry facts across conversations
The agent should keep the preference in a scratchpad so that it is repeated in each and every new chat
quiz.explain: The gap is cross-conversation recall, which memory scoped to a subject covers. A larger session or summaries only help within one interaction, and a scratchpad lives in the window and disappears with it.

quiz.q: A support agent stores customer facts as rows in Lakebase Postgres. A user asks, "What is my current plan tier?" and the tier is one column on the customer row. Which retrieval fits?
choices: A SQL lookup on the customer key for the exact value
A similarity search over embedded notes, ranked by closeness of meaning to the question asked
A hybrid keyword-similarity query, merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, over free-text notes about the customer
A language-model summary of the full history, trusted to mention the current tier correctly
quiz.explain: When the key and field are known, a structured query is exact and cheap. Similarity ranking adds uncertainty for a single column value, and summaries may omit it.

days.recap: Choose the store by scope (interaction or subject), move durable multi-step state into Delta tables rather than the window, and match retrieval to the query: SQL for exact fields, semantic search for paraphrase, filters for ownership.

days.title: Comparing Runs, Static versus Dynamic Retrieval, Over- and Under-Retrieval

concepts.heading: Choosing the most reliable configuration in MLflow 3
concepts.body: mlflow.genai.evaluate() runs an app over an evaluation dataset with scorers, such as LLM judges and code checks, and records one trace per row with feedback in an evaluation run. The docs tutorial compares versions in the experiment's Evaluation runs view: tick the runs, choose Compare from the Actions menu, and open the full traces for the same request from each run to see what each version put into the context. Reliability needs more than one mean. Model outputs vary between runs, so repeat the same dataset and scorers and weigh the spread against the average; treating the spread as a stability measure is generally accepted evaluation practice, not a Databricks rule. A high mean with a wide range depends on luck. A dataset can only show what it exercises: if every question is answerable from its own text, memory on and off will tie, so add rows whose answer depends on an earlier conversation. At equal quality, prefer the configuration that uses less context, because lower cost and latency and less distraction are real advantages.

concepts.heading: Static versus dynamic retrieval from Lakebase
concepts.body: Static and dynamic retrieval are the exam's vocabulary; the Databricks docs do not define them. Static retrieval means the application fetches a known, fixed piece of memory with a predetermined query before the model call and places it in the prompt. It is predictable and adds no model round trip. Dynamic retrieval means the model decides during the run to call a lookup tool and forms the query itself. It loads only what the task needs, but adds a tool-call round trip and depends on the model choosing to call it. Lakebase is managed Postgres, which suits a fixed keyed lookup before every request. The rule of thumb: always needed and small means static; sometimes needed, large or unpredictable means dynamic. Hybrid designs follow, loading a few stable fields such as segment or language every turn and leaving a large note history behind a tool. If traces show the agent skipping a dynamic lookup, the main lever is the tool description, which should say what the memory holds and which questions need it. Fields needed on nearly every call should become static.

concepts.heading: Over-retrieval and context pollution
concepts.body: Over-retrieval and under-retrieval are generally accepted retrieval terms and the exam's convention; the Databricks docs do not define them. Over-retrieval, also called context pollution, means too many or weakly relevant memories are injected. They spend the attention budget, distract the model, and let an old, unrelated fact steer the answer. Agent memory is retrieved by semantic search, so closest means most similar, not necessarily relevant, and a fixed count such as the 25 nearest memories always injects something even when only a few matter. In a trace the signs are many returned items with few used, an unrelated detail echoed in the answer, and prompt size that grows with the store. Pollution also comes from size, not only count: a memory entry that holds a whole transcript carries thousands of unrelated tokens around one useful sentence. Store one durable fact per entry (a design practice), since memory is meant for distilled facts and the raw record belongs in sessions. Other generally accepted fixes are a smaller cap, a relevance threshold and a query that states the current task.

concepts.heading: Under-retrieval and tuning both failures
concepts.body: Under-retrieval means a relevant memory exists in the store but never reaches the prompt, so the agent behaves as if it had forgotten. Typical causes are a similarity threshold so strict that a short query like what should I cook tonight never matches a stored sentence saying the user is vegetarian, a query that never mentions the constraint, and a cap so low that relevant items rank below it. Diagnose before changing anything by comparing three things in the trace: what the store contains, what retrieval returned and what the answer used. If the store has the fact but retrieval returns nothing, the gap is in retrieval. If the store lacks it, the gap is in writing, meaning the memory pipeline or the agent's memory writing. Lowering a cap trades one failure for the other, since a fixed small number cannot suit a question needing one fact and another needing three. Combine a relevance gate, which lets the count follow how many items are relevant, with a moderate cap, and rerun the same evaluation dataset and judges to confirm both improved.

examPoints: Compare MLflow 3 evaluation runs on the same dataset and scorers, look at spread as well as mean, and open traces to see the context; at equal quality pick the leaner configuration.

Static retrieval (fixed query before the call) suits small, always-needed memory; dynamic retrieval (a tool) suits large or rarely needed memory and depends on the tool description and the model's choice.
Over-retrieval is many items with few used; under-retrieval is a stored fact that never arrives. Fix with a relevance gate plus a moderate cap, one fact per entry, then re-evaluate both.

quiz.q: Three memory-injection configurations were each run five times in MLflow on the same dataset and judges. Configuration X has mean correctness 0.86 with scores from 0.84 to 0.88. Configuration Y has mean 0.88 with scores from 0.70 to 0.97. Configuration Z has mean 0.79 with scores from 0.78 to 0.80. Which is the most reliable, and why?
choices: Y, because the highest mean means it will be right most often in production
Z, because the narrowest range shows the most dependable behaviour of the three
Y, because its best single run shows the ceiling the configuration can reach
X, because a high mean with a narrow range is both strong and dependable
quiz.explain: Reliability weighs the spread against the mean. X is nearly as accurate as Y and far more stable, while Z is stable but lower. Y's wide range shows its result depends on the run.

quiz.q: An assistant injects the 25 closest memories from its Lakebase-backed memory store into every request. As the store grew, answers cited an irrelevant old fact. Which change best addresses the cause?
choices: Raise the cap to 50 so that the relevant memory is certain to be included every time
Remove the semantic search so memories are chosen at random for each request
Add a relevance gate and moderate cap, then rerun the same evaluation
Switch to a model with a larger window so that all 25 memories fit comfortably
quiz.explain: The symptom is over-retrieval: weakly relevant items fill the window. A relevance gate lets the count follow relevance, a cap bounds the worst case, and the rerun checks that recall did not drop. More items or a bigger window keep the distraction.

days.recap: Judge configurations on mean and spread with traces, match static or dynamic retrieval to how predictable the need is, and tune over- and under-retrieval together with a relevance gate, a moderate cap and one fact per memory.

days.title: Durable Memory across Sessions and Resolving Intent before Retrieval

concepts.heading: Configuring persistent memory across sessions
concepts.body: The stateful-agents page lists the pieces you configure. A session store keeps each interaction's state. A memory store holds durable facts. A memory pipeline reads the conversations in the session store, extracts durable facts, writes them to the memory store, on demand or on a schedule, and consolidates them over time, without adding memory-writing tools to your agent. The tutorial on adding sessions and memory to an existing agent connects those three; the Agent Bricks quickstart builds a new agent with them already set up. Consolidation matters because recall is semantic search: if a nightly pipeline writes forty near-identical entries for one preference, they all score high and occupy every slot of a small result list, pushing a different relevant fact out. Merge duplicates at write time so each slot carries a different fact. Because the stores are independent, a retired agent's session store can be deleted without losing the memories, and clearing a memory is a separate action. Managed agent memory governed by Unity Catalog is documented as Legacy and not recommended for new agents, so it is never the answer for a new design.

concepts.heading: Subject scope and store permissions
concepts.body: Memory is scoped to a subject, not an interaction. A common bug is keying memories by the current chat identifier. A fact then behaves like session state and can only be found from the chat that created it, so a size preference set on Monday is unknown in Wednesday's new chat. The docs state the scoping. Treating each customer as a subject, written and recalled by that subject so one customer's memories never reach another, is a design practice built on it. Databricks documents permissions for memory and session stores: you grant, inspect, list and revoke access to them. Two layers therefore exist. Store permissions decide which identities can read or write the stores at all. Subject-scoped recall, in practice, decides which memories a given request may see. Apply least privilege, granting only the agents and people who need a store and revoking when they no longer do. A prompt instruction such as only discuss this customer is not an access control, because the memories would already be in the model's context by the time the instruction is read.

concepts.heading: Where intent is resolved in the pipeline
concepts.body: Retrieval can only be as good as its query. A message like what did they decide about it has nothing an index can match, and embedding it raw returns noise. Resolving intent means turning the user message plus session state into a clear standalone query, and when needed choosing the source, before any retrieval runs. The stage is generally accepted pipeline vocabulary and the exam's convention; the Databricks docs do not define it. The order is: receive the message with session state, resolve intent by expanding references, disambiguating names and choosing between structured lookup and semantic search, retrieve with the resolved query, then inject the result. The session store is the natural input because it holds the conversation so far. Doing it after retrieval is too late, because the window already holds whatever the raw query matched. An ambiguous request such as the numbers for Apollo, where a project and a customer share the name, cannot be fixed by any retrieval setting; use session context or ask a short clarifying question rather than retrieving both meanings and inviting the model to blend them.

concepts.heading: Resolving intent only when it pays
concepts.body: Intent resolution costs a model call and latency, so apply it where it adds value. A self-contained message such as what is my current plan tier can be retrieved as written. A message with unresolved references, or one that could match several entities or sources, needs the step. A practical design puts a cheap check in front, either rules or a small classifier. Clear messages go straight to retrieval, and ambiguous ones are rewritten or answered with a clarifying question first. That keeps the benefits for the minority that needs them without taxing the majority; this is an engineering trade-off in the exam's convention, not a Databricks rule. The benefits when the step runs are two: a specific query retrieves less noise, so less attention budget is wasted and over-retrieval falls, and the resolved query can be routed to the method that fits, a structured query for a single stored field or semantic search for a vague recollection. It does not remove the need to evaluate retrieval or to store distilled memories.

examPoints: Persistent memory is session store plus memory store plus a memory pipeline that distills and consolidates; merge duplicates at write time and never choose the Legacy managed memory for a new agent.
Key memories by subject, not chat identifier; control access with store permissions and subject-scoped recall, not with prompt instructions.
Resolve intent after the message and session state arrive and before retrieval; it is the exam's term, and it can be skipped for self-contained messages to save a model call.

quiz.q: A shopping agent writes memories keyed by the current chat identifier. A customer sets a size preference on Monday, opens a new chat on Wednesday, and the agent asks for the size again. What is the fix?
choices: Scope memories to the customer as the subject, for writing and recalling alike
Extend the Monday session store so its transcript is replayed into every future chat automatically for the user
Increase the number of memories retrieved per request until the preference finally appears
Store the preference in a scratchpad inside the context window of each new chat the customer opens
quiz.explain: Memory is scoped to a subject, so keying by chat makes a durable fact behave like session state. A longer transcript, a bigger cap or a scratchpad does not give cross-conversation recall.

quiz.q: A support agent answers accurately but off target. A user writes "What did they decide about it?" after discussing a vendor contract earlier in the chat, and the pipeline embeds that raw sentence to query memory. Where should the fix go?
choices: After retrieval, with a reranker that reorders whatever the raw sentence happened to match
In a standalone query built from message and session state before retrieval
In the memory pipeline, which should store more entries so that the raw sentence matches them
In the system prompt, which should tell the agent to ignore any unrelated memories it receives
quiz.explain: Intent resolution belongs after the message and session state are available and before retrieval, so the query is clear. A reranker cannot recover content the raw query never matched, and the other two do not repair the query.

days.recap: Persistent memory needs sessions, a memory store and a pipeline that distills and consolidates; scope it by subject and permissions, and resolve intent into a clear query before retrieval, skipping the step for clear messages.

days.title: Progressive Disclosure of MCP Tools and Tool Descriptions

concepts.heading: Why raw tool dumps cost context
concepts.body: Databricks documents the Model Context Protocol as the way an agent queries data, searches documents and calls external services. Databricks-provided MCP servers (Genie One, GitHub, Slack and others), registered servers and custom servers hosted on Databricks Apps all expose tools, and by MCP convention each tool reaches the model as a name, a description and a parameter schema (the Databricks pages do not spell this out). If the agent loads every definition from every server at the start, those schemas travel in every model call whether or not the request uses them. That spends the attention budget before the user's question is read and leaves less room for the task. A tool result is context too: a generic SQL tool that returns four thousand rows pushes them all into the window and leaves the arithmetic to the model. A purpose-built tool that aggregates in the warehouse and returns three rows is cheaper and more reliable. The wording progressive disclosure, scoping tool results and attention budget is the exam guide's vocabulary and generally accepted context-engineering practice. The Databricks docs do not define it as a setting.

concepts.heading: The staged approach and its cost
concepts.body: Progressive disclosure loads tool information in stages, each adding only what the next decision needs. Stage one is a compact index: a name plus a one-line purpose for each tool or server. Stage two happens after the agent selects a tool: a lookup step returns that tool's full parameter schema. Stage three is the call itself, whose result should also be scoped, for example a list of order ids and statuses plus a separate detail call for one order. Count it: a catalog of 60 tools at about 500 tokens per schema costs 30,000 tokens as a dump. Staged, it costs 60 index lines of about 20 tokens plus 3 schemas, about 2,700 tokens. The price is one extra round trip per tool used. The agent also has to know the protocol, so a few lines in the prompt must say that the index is not enough to call a tool and that the lookup comes first. Without it the agent guesses arguments and gets validation errors.

concepts.heading: Hot tools and permitted tools
concepts.body: Staging is a trade of steps for tokens, so it should not cover everything. Tools used in nearly every conversation, such as order lookup in a support chat, belong in the always-loaded layer: deferring them adds a round trip every time and saves little. Rarely used tools in the long tail go behind the index. A second lever is not exposing tools nobody needs. The Databricks docs say Databricks-provided and registered MCP servers use Unity Catalog permissions, and that a registered MCP exposes all its tools by default unless you select them. Unselected tools do not appear in tools/list, and calls to them are rejected. A policy can deny a tool for one agent, but the tool stays in the list, so only tool selection removes its definition. If nobody needs 12 of an MCP's 30 tools, deselect them: the 12 definitions leave every call and the model cannot choose them. A prompt line listing forbidden tools leaves the definitions in the window. Choosing the smallest useful tool set as a context strategy is the exam's convention, not a documented Databricks feature.

concepts.heading: Ambiguous tool descriptions
concepts.body: The model picks a tool mainly from its name and description, and fills arguments from parameter names and descriptions. When two descriptions say nearly the same thing, nothing separates them and the choice becomes close to random. Overlap takes several forms. Two near-identical sentences, such as one tool looking up customer information and another retrieving account information for a customer. A superset tool, such as a billing history tool whose description is the union of an invoice tool and a payments tool. Identical names from different servers, such as a generic search tool on both GitHub and Slack. Parameters both described as the id. Read the descriptions as the model does and ask which ones fit a sample question. The fix is to state what the tool returns, its key input, when to prefer it and when not to, plus formats such as a C- or ACC- prefix. Random names, identical text or a rule to choose freely do not separate anything. Overlap analysis is exam vocabulary, not a Databricks-defined term.

examPoints: Progressive disclosure shows a compact tool index first and loads a tool's full schema only after the agent selects it, so tool tokens follow the tools used, not the tools that exist; the cost is an extra round trip, and the agent must be told the protocol.

Keep frequently used tools always loaded, put the long tail behind the index, select only the tools callers need on a registered MCP (unselected tools drop out of tools/list), and scope tool results (aggregate server-side, return a summary plus a detail call).

Confusing tools are fixed by contrastive descriptions: what each returns, its input and format, when to use it instead of the neighbor, and system or item type for same-named tools; renaming to meaningless names or duplicating text does not help.

quiz.q: An agent reaches 60 registered tools and every model call starts with all their names, descriptions and schemas. The team adopts progressive disclosure. What does the window hold before the agent has picked a tool?
choices: The full schemas of the ten most used tools, with the other fifty hidden until requested by exact name
A compact index of tool names and one-line descriptions, with a full schema fetched only after selection
Only the user's question, so the agent has to guess a tool name and learn its parameters from the error
Every full schema with the parameter descriptions removed, so that all 60 tools fit in a smaller footprint
quiz.explain: The first stage is a short index that answers which tool to use; the full schema is loaded for the chosen tool only. Hiding all tool information leaves nothing to choose from, and stripped schemas still load every tool.

quiz.q: An agent has find_customer ("Looks up customer information.") and get_account ("Retrieves account information for a customer."). It calls them almost at random for a billing address question. Which change fixes the confusion?
choices: Add the same worked example call for both tools to the system prompt so the model sees how each one is invoked
Rename the tools tool_a and tool_b so that the names cannot suggest anything that might mislead the model
Append synonyms of customer and account to both descriptions so that every question matches both strongly
Rewrite each description to state what it returns, its key input and when to use it instead of the other tool
quiz.explain: The descriptions overlap, so the fix is contrastive wording that tells the model which tool returns the billing address and which input each needs. The same example, meaningless names or more synonyms leave nothing that separates the tools.

days.recap: Tool definitions and tool results are context: stage them with a compact index, a schema lookup and scoped results, keep hot tools loaded, expose only permitted tools, and write contrastive descriptions. Progressive disclosure is the exam's term, not a Databricks setting.

days.title: Clearing Tool Results, Unity Catalog Function Tools and Agent Skills

concepts.heading: Which raw tool results can be cleared
concepts.body: In a long task the largest items in the message history are usually raw tool outputs, and they matter most in the turn that produced them. Clearing a tool result means removing its bulky payload from the window. The terms tool result clearing and message history pressure belong to the exam guide and to generally accepted context-engineering practice. The Databricks docs do not define them. A result is a good candidate when it is large and nothing the task still needs exists only inside it. Candidates are a 30,000-character JSON whose three order ids and totals are already written into the plan, a broad query superseded by a narrower one, and a 9,000-token column listing after the agent chose two tables and noted their columns. Poor candidates are a small result holding the only copy of a value the final answer must report, the user's region used as a filter in every remaining step, and the result of the call made one step ago that the agent has not analyzed yet. Size alone does not decide; dependence does.

concepts.heading: Clearing policies that keep a way back
concepts.body: Clearing is a policy as well as a technique. Decide how soon each result is needed again. An inventory agent that diffs each new result against the previous two keeps the three newest in full and replaces the older ones with placeholders. Clearing the newest results, keeping all forty, or clearing everything immediately each fail in a different way. The placeholder matters: if a cleared result leaves no trace, the history looks as if the call never happened and the agent repeats it. A placeholder names the tool, the arguments and the key findings, which costs a few tokens. When the raw rows are also stored in a Delta table, the placeholder can hold the table name, the row count and the findings, and the agent can reload exact rows later with a just-in-time query. Truncating a JSON to its first characters, summarizing and discarding the table, or moving rows into the system prompt do not keep that path back. Prompt rules such as never call a tool twice break legitimate refreshes. These policies are generally accepted practice, not Databricks features.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Unity Catalog function as a tool
concepts.body: The Databricks page on agent tools with Unity Catalog functions says to use them when the agent needs to run predefined logic, such as a SQL query whose parameters the agent supplies, and to start with MCP servers for other tools. Calling an existing function needs EXECUTE on it plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parent catalog and schema, so access is governed in Unity Catalog. Registered functions have named parameters and a return type, so a choice can be judged from them. Ask three things. Functional fit: does the tool do the step, such as a calc_discount function when the agent already holds the order total and tier. Input and output compatibility: can the agent supply every parameter from what it has, and does the output match the next tool's parameter, such as an ISO 8601 string for a start_time STRING. Task requirements: a fixed approved calculation with region and quarter parameters beats a tool that accepts any SQL text. Prefer narrow typed inputs, allowed values and small returns, such as a single status value, over free-text filters or whole-table returns. Narrow-input design is generally accepted practice.

concepts.heading: Packaging rarely used instructions as Agent Skills
concepts.body: The Databricks page on extending Genie Code with agent skills says skills follow the open Agent Skills standard and package domain-specific knowledge and workflows, with guidance, best practices, reusable code and executable scripts. Unlike custom instructions, which are applied globally, skills are loaded automatically and only in the relevant context, based on the request and the skill's description. That keeps the context window efficient, which is why a rarely used procedure belongs in a skill and not in an always-on prompt. Each skill has its own folder with a required SKILL.md whose frontmatter has a name and a description, then Markdown instructions; scripts and reference files go in the folder and are referenced by relative paths. The docs give a workspace skill example of PII handling that masks sensitive columns. The description is the loading trigger, so vague wording causes both missed and false loads, and the docs advise clear names and descriptions and focused skills. Rules that apply to every request, such as tone or confidentiality, stay in the always-on instructions. Calling this progressive disclosure is the exam's framing.

examPoints: Clear a raw tool result only when it is large and what the task needs is already captured elsewhere; superseded and already extracted results qualify, while a sole copy of a needed value or the latest unanalyzed result does not.

Replace cleared results with placeholders naming the tool, arguments and key findings, keep the newest results the next step compares in full, and for results stored in Delta put the table name in the placeholder so the agent can query again.

Choose a Unity Catalog function tool by functional fit and input/output compatibility with narrow typed parameters; package rarely used workflows as skills (SKILL.md with name and description, loaded when relevant) and keep rules for every request in the system prompt.

quiz.q: A research agent nears its context limit. The history holds a 30,000-character JSON from get_orders returned 25 turns ago. The three order ids and totals needed from it are already in the agent's plan, and the raw JSON will not be used again. Which action frees space without hurting the task?
choices: Clear the raw result, keep the plan entries and leave a short note of the call
Truncate the JSON to its first 2,000 characters so part of every old result stays available
Clear the agent's reasoning messages from the last ten turns, since reasoning matters less than data
Delete the plan entries together with the JSON, because the plan only repeats what the JSON contained
quiz.explain: The needed facts live in the plan, so the bulky payload can go while a short note records the call. Truncation leaves partial data, reasoning may hold unrecorded decisions, and deleting the plan removes the only copy of the facts.

quiz.q: A team packaged a data-quality workflow as a skill whose description reads "Helpful workflow stuff." The agent ignores it for data-quality requests and sometimes applies it to unrelated tasks, although the SKILL.md instructions are correct. What fixes the loading behavior?
choices: Merge it with the team's other skills into one large skill, so that the agent only has a single description to match
Copy the instructions into the system prompt as well, so that they apply whatever the description says
Rewrite the name and description to say what the skill does and when to use it, for one workflow
Move every referenced script into SKILL.md so that the skill loads as one file
quiz.explain: The agent decides from the name and description whether to load a skill, so a specific description fixes both misses and false loads. Merging, duplicating into the prompt or inlining scripts all increase context or blur the trigger.

days.recap: Clear large raw tool results once their needed facts are captured, and leave placeholders with a path back. Pick Unity Catalog function tools by fit and compatibility, and move rarely used workflows into skills with precise descriptions.

days.title: Compaction: Finding Lost Information and Tuning the Prompt

concepts.heading: What compaction is, and what it loses
concepts.body: Compaction replaces older history with a summary so a long task can continue inside the window. The exam guide's terms, compaction, summarization and trimming, are generally accepted context-engineering practice; the Databricks docs do not define compaction or describe a compaction prompt, so treat them as the exam's vocabulary and not as a Databricks feature. A summarizer left without guidance tends to keep the narrative and drop exact strings, because they look like detail. The symptoms after compaction point to what was dropped. An agent that asks again for a stack trace and file path lost exact strings. An agent that writes to orders_prod after being told to work only in orders_dev lost a constraint. An agent that stops and asks what to do next lost its remaining steps. An agent that repeats a failed approach lost negative results. An agent that cannot give a growth rate lost exact figures. Every one is a category of information that a paraphrase cannot rebuild.

concepts.heading: Diagnose, then revise the prompt
concepts.body: The efficient order of work has three steps. First compare the summary with the raw history, which an MLflow trace preserves, and name the category that is missing. Second, change the compaction prompt so that this category is required: keep error messages, paths and identifiers verbatim; keep the user's goal, constraints and prohibitions stated explicitly; include a section for current state and remaining steps in order; list approaches tried and why they failed; keep figures with units and labels. Third, re-run and check that the failing questions are now answerable. This diagnose-and-revise loop is generally accepted practice. Each fix adds a few lines to the summary, so the token cost barely moves. Wrong turns are easy to name. Making the summary shorter or friendlier does not restore data. Compacting earlier removes more detail. Deleting the oldest turns has no judgment. Rounding numbers destroys the values. A generic warning in the system prompt does not name the table that was lost. Telling the agent to refuse the question hides the symptom.

concepts.heading: Tuning order: recall first, then precision
concepts.body: Define two measures on a saved trace. Recall is the share of facts that later steps need which survive in the summary, for example 34 of 40 is 85 percent. Precision is how much of the summary is useful, with repeated or superfluous output counting against it, for example 8 of 20 sentences only restate earlier ones. The exam guide's order is to maximize recall first and then improve precision.
