A short summary hides what is missing, while noise in a long summary is easy to see and cut, so trimming before recall is complete only hides the gaps. In practice, build a checklist of the facts each trace's later steps use and score every revision against it. Change one instruction at a time on the same traces so an effect can be tied to a change. Include varied traces, not only one clean run. When a precision edit such as drop redundant tool output costs an order id, narrow the rule to duplicates and failed output and add a keep list for identifiers. Do not revert everything. This method is generally accepted practice, not a documented Databricks procedure.

concepts.heading: Trimming heuristics or real compaction
concepts.body: A hard-coded trimming rule, such as keep the last 15 messages or drop tool results older than 10 steps, needs no extra model call and behaves the same way every time. It is enough when relevance follows a simple pattern, usually recency. A FAQ agent answering independent questions fits, and so does a nightly batch where only the status line at a known position of each log matters; a parser can keep that line and clear the rest. It fails when relevance depends on content, not age. A migration agent that learned in step 2 that dates are stored in local time needs that fact in step 70, and a user correction from the first third of a run must survive whenever it was given. Window pressure alone does not justify a new approach, since every long run fills the window. The deciding fact is the information relevance pattern. Mixed histories can use a hybrid: a rule clears used tool outputs, and a content-aware compaction keeps the small dialogue of constraints. Raising the window size or changing N only delays the loss.

examPoints: After a compaction failure, compare the summary with the raw history, name the dropped category (exact strings, constraints, remaining steps, failed approaches, figures) and require that category in the compaction prompt without making the summary much longer.

Tune recall first (capture everything later steps need, scored against a checklist of facts from saved traces), then improve precision (merge repeated output, drop retries), one change at a time on the same traces, and narrow a precision rule that costs recall instead of reverting it.

Use a trimming heuristic when relevance follows recency or a fixed structure; use content-aware compaction when an early finding or correction can matter late, and combine the two when the history has parts with different patterns.

quiz.q: A migration agent was told in turn 3: "Do not touch orders_prod; work only in orders_dev." After its history was compacted the agent wrote to orders_prod. The summary said only "the user asked for a migration of the orders tables." What should change in the compaction step?
choices: Add "be careful with production tables" to the system prompt and leave the compaction prompt as it is
Remove every user message from the summarizer's input, since user messages are the source of conflicting instructions
Raise the sampling temperature so the agent tries different actions after each compaction step
Require the summary to keep the user's goal, constraints and prohibitions, stated explicitly with table names
quiz.explain: The constraint was lost in compaction, so the compaction prompt must name constraints as a category to keep. A generic warning does not name the table, and dropping user messages or adding randomness removes or ignores the rule.

quiz.q: After two tuning rounds a compaction prompt keeps every fact that later steps use in five sample traces, but summaries repeat the same verbose query output three times and include full retry text. What is the right next iteration?
choices: Remove the instruction listing what to preserve so that the summarizer can drop the noisy output itself
Add instructions that merge repeated output and drop retry text, then re-check the same traces
Replace the prompt with a rule that keeps only the last ten messages of the history in every case
Raise the maximum summary size so the repeated text fits, since the facts are already preserved
quiz.explain: Recall is acceptable, so the next step is a targeted precision edit followed by a re-check that no needed fact vanished. Removing the keep list or switching to a last-N rule risks recall, and a larger cap accepts the noise.

days.recap: Compaction failures show up as a missing category of information, so diagnose against the raw trace and require that category in the prompt. Tune recall before precision with measurable checks, and use fixed trimming only when relevance follows a regular pattern.

days.title: What to Keep, What to Drop and Aggressive vs Conservative Compaction

concepts.heading: Load-bearing content versus safe-to-remove content
concepts.body: Content is safe to remove during compaction when no downstream step depends on it, because it is repeated, because its useful part was extracted and the way to reproduce it is kept, or because it is metadata nobody reads. Content is load-bearing when a later step reads it. The categories below are the exam guide's convention and generally accepted practice; the Databricks docs do not define a keep list. Keep: user instructions, corrections and prohibitions that are still active; identifiers and values a later call will use, such as a transaction id returned 12 turns ago; open plan steps; decisions with their reasons; records of failed approaches. Usually removable: raw HTML or a 3,000-row result already reduced to the needed figures with the query text kept; identical boilerplate prepended to every tool result after the first copy; pleasantries. An age rule that deletes old tool output can destroy the only copy of a pending value, so extract such values into the summary before clearing the output.

concepts.heading: Operational metadata and how to prove removal is safe
concepts.body: Some content exists for the developer, not the agent. A wrapper that appends latency_ms, tokens and request_id to every tool result adds tokens that no later step reads. The Databricks tracing overview states that MLflow Tracing records the inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every intermediate step, so the same data survives outside the context window and removing it from the agent's history costs nothing. The test is simple: does any downstream step read it, and does a better record exist? To prove it for a new category, such as retrieved passages the agent quotes in earlier answers, do not rely on size, age or the model's own opinion. Size says nothing about dependence, old passages can be cited again, and a model's self-report about its needs is unreliable. Replay saved traces with the category removed and compare downstream steps and final answers with the originals; a changed step or answer means the removal is unsafe. MLflow evaluation on a fixed set of traces makes that comparison repeatable. This replay method is generally accepted practice.

concepts.heading: Aggressive versus conservative compaction
concepts.body: Compaction posture is a trade between tokens and fidelity. Aggressive compaction compresses hard: fewer tokens on every later call, lower cost and latency, but a higher chance of losing a subtle qualifier, an exception or a negation. Conservative compaction keeps more detail: higher fidelity, but longer summaries that cost more on each call and use more of the attention budget. Neither guarantees correct answers, and neither removes the need to measure downstream accuracy. The right posture follows the cost of an error against the cost of tokens. A triage agent classifying thousands of low-stakes tickets per hour, where a missed detail costs a minor re-ask, should compress aggressively. A claims agent where a missed exclusion clause can cause a wrong payout should keep clauses and qualifiers verbatim and accept the cost. Neither extreme is mandatory. The posture is the exam's convention, and the Databricks docs set no compaction level.

concepts.heading: Tiered compaction and deciding with data
concepts.body: Between the extremes, a tiered prompt compresses by category. Pin what is costly to lose, such as clauses, exceptions, constraints and identifiers, verbatim, and compress routine narrative and bulk output hard. Since most tokens in a trace are routine, most of the savings remain while the dangerous losses are blocked. Alternating postures on a timer, compressing the first half hard, running conservative compaction on every call while halving the documents read, or having a human review summaries all fail: losses depend on content, older material is where an early clause sits, and reviewers cannot restore details that are no longer in the summary. To choose a level for a new agent, use data. Run the same saved tasks at several compaction levels with MLflow evaluation, whose traces record token usage and cost for each step, compare task success with token cost, and choose the cheapest level that meets the quality bar. Copying another agent's posture or picking the best-written summaries does not measure that. The decision rule is the exam's convention.

examPoints: Keep active constraints and corrections, pending identifiers and values, open plan steps, decisions and failed approaches; remove duplicates, boilerplate, pleasantries and raw output whose conclusion and reproduction path are kept; extract values before clearing by age.

Operational metadata that no step reads, such as latency and token lines, is safe to remove because MLflow Tracing records latency, token usage and cost; prove a new category is safe by replaying saved traces without it and comparing downstream steps and answers.

Aggressive compaction fits low-stakes, high-volume work; conservative fits costly errors; a tiered prompt pins critical categories verbatim and compresses the rest, and the level is chosen by comparing task success and token cost on the same tasks.

quiz.q: An agent's wrapper appends a debug line such as latency_ms=412 tokens=1860 request_id=7f3a to every tool result. The lines are a sizeable share of the history, no later step reads them, and MLflow Tracing records the same information. Can they be removed during compaction?
choices: No, because request ids must stay in the history for the agent to resend a request when a call fails
Yes, because no step reads them and MLflow Tracing already records latency, token usage and cost
Yes, but only after the agent has repeated each figure in its own words so that a copy of every value remains
No, because latency and token figures can change the agent's choice of tool and must stay in the history
quiz.explain: The lines are unread by the agent and a better record exists in the trace, so removing them saves tokens at no cost. Restating them keeps the noise, and retries and tool choice do not depend on these figures here.

quiz.q: A long-running legal-research agent reads dozens of documents. Aggressive compaction was cheap but sometimes lost an exception clause. Conservative compaction fixed that but doubled token cost. Which design keeps most of the savings and the safety?
choices: Run conservative compaction on every call, and halve the number of documents the agent reads in each session
Compress aggressively in the second half of each task and conservatively in the first half
Compact aggressively, but keep clauses, exceptions and constraints verbatim and compress routine text
Alternate aggressive and conservative compaction on a timer, so the average cost falls between the two
quiz.explain: Pinning the costly categories verbatim blocks the observed failure while routine content still shrinks. The other designs cut coverage, compress old clauses or merely average the risk without regard to content.

days.recap: Remove what no later step reads or what is captured and reproducible, keep constraints, pending values, open steps and failed approaches, and verify by replaying traces. Choose aggressive or conservative compaction by the cost of an error, usually tiered, and decide with task success against token cost.

days.title: Multi-Agent Failures: Shared Context, Dispatch and Propagation

concepts.heading: Where This Material Comes From
concepts.body: Section 7 is 13 percent of the exam, and it rests on a different kind of source than most of the other sections. The exam guide defines the scenarios, and the Databricks documentation does not define a dispatch protocol, a context propagation mechanism or a schema for sub-agent messages. Treat the terms in this domain as the exam guide's convention and as generally accepted context-engineering practice, never as a Databricks feature you configure. The one documented piece of support is the MLflow Tracing overview: a trace records the inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every intermediate step, which makes it the evidence you read when you diagnose a multi-agent system. Genie also has a multi-agent page, but it describes a Public Preview capability, so it is never the answer to a question here. The reasoning style is the same as in earlier days: name the symptom, find what information was missing or oversized in some agent's window, and choose the smallest change that fixes it without enlarging any window.

concepts.heading: Insufficient Shared Context and Its Symptoms
concepts.body: A coordinating agent splits a task and sub-agents work on the pieces. Each sub-agent starts with an empty window apart from what it is given, so every fact, constraint and decision it was not given is something it must assume. The exam names three symptoms of that gap. Inconsistent outputs: one writer uses fiscal quarters and another calendar quarters, or two agents use different words for the same entity. Conflicting decisions: a pricing agent accepts a discount that a legal agent, working at the same time, rules out. Degraded reliability: the result changes from run to run because each agent infers what it was never told. The pattern to recognise is agents that each behave sensibly alone and disagree together. Other failures look similar but have other causes: a slow external API, a transient service error and a high token bill do not come from missing shared facts, and passing more context does not fix them. Increasing temperature, swapping models or merging everything into one agent does not supply the missing fact either.

concepts.heading: Dispatch: Task Message Versus Trace
concepts.body: The guide's central diagnosis is a sub-agent that receives an individual task message rather than the full agent trace at dispatch. The task message tells it what to do; the trace tells it what the coordinator already decided, ruled out and learned. Without the trace the sub-agent falls back on defaults, for example quoting a standard refund policy that planning had already rejected. The constraint in the question is usually that the fix must not expand each sub-agent's context window. Pasting a raw, long trace in front of every task breaks that rule, and it also buries the needed facts among exploration steps. The configuration that satisfies both goals is to dispatch a compacted, relevance-filtered version of the trace: the decisions, constraints, definitions and results that apply to this sub-task, in condensed form, with the task message on top. Compaction here is the same technique as in Section 6, applied at the hand-off. This dispatch rule is the guide's convention, not a Databricks setting. To confirm the diagnosis, compare each sub-agent span's recorded input in the MLflow trace with the coordinator's earlier steps and look for what never arrived.

concepts.heading: Context Propagation That Prevents Conflicts
concepts.body: When a multi-agent system produces conflicting outputs, the exam asks which propagation change would most likely prevent the conflict. Two rules cover most items. First, order dependent work. If a staffing plan depends on a demand forecast, do not dispatch both in parallel; run the forecast first and pass its assumptions on, or keep the decision in a shared record every agent reads. Parallel dispatch is correct only for independent tasks. Second, send conclusions together with their basis. A verdict such as margin is acceptable, stripped of the assumption that returns were excluded, can be applied outside the conditions that make it valid; the receiving agent needs the decision, assumptions, constraints and the evidence it rests on, and not the exploration that produced them. This links to context clash, the exam's term for parts of the context that disagree. Prevention beats repair: a later review pass finds the conflict after both agents did the work, while a voting step or a lower temperature only chooses among conflicting inputs and supplies no missing fact. These propagation rules are the exam's convention and general practice.

examPoints: Missing shared context shows as inconsistent outputs, conflicting decisions or run-to-run unreliability; slow APIs, transient errors and cost are different problems.
Sub-agents given only a task message miss earlier decisions; fix it by dispatching a compacted, relevance-filtered trace, not a bigger window or a raw paste.
Order dependent tasks and pass conclusions with their assumptions; these dispatch and propagation rules are the exam's convention, not a documented Databricks feature.

quiz.q: A coordinator dispatches a sub-agent with only the message "Draft the reply for ticket 4411". The coordinator's trace shows the customer's contract was already found to be legacy, so the standard policy was ruled out, yet the draft quotes the standard policy. The sub-agent's window cannot grow. Which change fits?
choices: Switch the sub-agent to a model with a larger window so the full raw trace can be pasted in front of the task
Send the task with a condensed trace slice holding the contract finding and the rejected policy
Add a second instruction sentence so that the sub-agent infers the contract type from the ticket text alone
Let the sub-agent ask the user which policy applies whenever a decision seems to be missing from its message
quiz.explain: The sub-agent lacked decisions the coordinator had already made. A condensed, relevant slice of the trace supplies them within the same window. A larger window with a raw trace is excluded by the constraint and buries the facts, an extra sentence cannot recover what the ticket text never contains, and asking the user repeats work the trace already holds.

quiz.q: A forecasting sub-agent assumes 12 percent demand growth while a staffing sub-agent, dispatched in parallel, plans on flat demand, and the combined plan contradicts itself. Which change most likely prevents the conflict?
choices: Add a review step after both agents finish, so the coordinator reconciles the two plans afterwards
Lower the temperature of both agents so that they pick the same demand assumption on every run
Give the staffing agent more search tools so it can find a demand source on its own
Run the forecast first and hand its growth assumption to the staffing agent before it starts
quiz.explain: The staffing result depends on the forecast, so the decision must reach it before it acts. A later review finds the conflict only after the work is done, lower temperature gives neither agent the other's assumption, and extra tools let each agent choose its own source and may yield a third figure.

days.recap: Missing shared context makes agents that are sensible alone disagree together. Dispatch a compacted, relevant trace slice instead of a bare task message or a raw paste, order dependent work, and send conclusions with their assumptions. All of this is the exam's convention; MLflow traces are the evidence.

days.title: Sub-Agent Outputs, Agent Boundaries and Long-Horizon Strategies

concepts.heading: Sub-Agent Output Design
concepts.body: The mirror image of dispatch is what a sub-agent sends back. A sub-agent does its heavy work in its own window, so it should return a distilled result rather than its raw tool output and reasoning. If five research sub-agents each return everything, the orchestrator saturates before it can synthesize, and compressing the text afterwards is too late because the tokens have already entered its window. The exam asks for the output design change that reduces orchestrator load without compromising task coherence, and both halves matter. A one-word verdict cuts load but removes the figures and the contradictions between sources, so coherence suffers. The balanced answer is a fixed output contract: a short, uniform structure with the fields the orchestrator will combine or compare, such as the verdict, key values, references to where the evidence is stored and any unresolved conflicts, with process narrative excluded. Uniform fields also make results easy to merge. The schema idea is the exam's convention and general practice, because the documentation defines no sub-agent output schema. The raw detail stays outside the orchestrator's window, in the sub-agent or in storage.

concepts.heading: Agent Boundary Placement
concepts.body: Every boundary between agents forces a handoff in which the sender compresses what it knows. The exam describes two opposite placement failures. Handoff compression overhead appears when a boundary cuts through tightly coupled work: a writer agent and a validator agent depend on the same reasoning, so every handoff needs a long summary and the receiver still asks for clarification. The signs in a trace are very long handoff messages plus follow-up questions between neighbours. The remedy is to keep the coupled steps in one agent or move the boundary to where dependency is low. Unmanageable context growth appears when a boundary is too wide: one operations agent owns research, report writing, compliance and replies, so unrelated tool results accumulate and accuracy falls over time. The remedy is to split along independent responsibilities so that each agent has a focused window and the coordinator exchanges short results. A larger window or a longer prompt only delays the second problem. Diagnose by reading the trace: long handoffs point to a boundary through coupled work, a swelling window points to a boundary that is too wide. This is the exam's convention.

concepts.heading: Matching the Long-Horizon Strategy
concepts.body: For tasks longer than one context window the exam compares three strategies and ties the choice to the dependency structure of the work. Compaction inside a single agent suits continuous work where each step builds on the running reasoning, since a summary can carry that thread forward. Structured note-taking, an external record of progress and facts that the agent writes and later re-reads, suits work made of discrete milestones where the exact state must survive context resets, for example a progress table of completed tables in a migration. Sub-agents with isolated contexts suit work that splits into independent branches, such as analysing twelve unrelated sources, where each branch is explored separately and reduced to findings. A mismatch produces a recognisable failure: compaction of a milestone list yields a summary like most tables are done, so finished items repeat or are skipped; compaction of independent branches lets every source crowd the others. Trimming oldest messages deletes exactly the early facts, and a bigger window only postpones the problem. These names and the matching rule are generally accepted practice and the exam's convention, not Databricks features.

examPoints: Make sub-agents return a fixed, compact schema (verdict, key values, evidence references, open conflicts); one-word verdicts lose coherence and raw returns saturate the orchestrator.
Long handoffs with follow-up questions mean a boundary through coupled work; a growing window of unrelated results means a boundary that is too wide.
Continuous reasoning fits compaction, discrete milestones fit note-taking, independent branches fit isolated sub-agents; none of this is a documented Databricks feature.

quiz.q: An orchestrator calls six research sub-agents that return their full tool output, and its context saturates before synthesis. A switch to one-word verdicts removed the saturation, but the report lost its supporting figures and cross-source contradictions went unnoticed. Which redesign fits?
choices: Each sub-agent returns a fixed short structure: verdict, key figures, evidence references, conflicts
Each sub-agent returns free-form prose limited to a paragraph, so the orchestrator can read the main points
The orchestrator re-reads all source documents itself after the verdicts arrive, to restore the figures
The team adds more sub-agents so that each one returns an even shorter and simpler verdict
quiz.explain: A fixed contract keeps load low and keeps the fields the report and the contradiction check need. Free prose has no uniform fields and may drop the figures again, re-reading the sources moves the whole load back to the orchestrator, and more sub-agents return still more text to combine.

quiz.q: An agent migrates sixty tables over many hours with compaction. After compactions it sometimes repeats a finished table or skips one, because the summary says most tables are done. Which replacement strategy fits, and why?
choices: Isolated sub-agents per table, because the failure comes from too little parallelism in the migration
Trimming the oldest messages, because the earliest turns hold only setup text that is no longer needed
A progress record read after each reset, since finished tables are discrete milestones
A larger context window, because the summary is only wrong while the window is too small to hold the history
quiz.explain: Compaction yields approximate prose, while a migration of discrete tables needs the exact set of finished ones, which an external structured record keeps across resets. Parallelism is not the problem, the oldest messages contain the completed tables so trimming erases them, and a larger window only delays the loss.

days.recap: Sub-agents return a compact fixed schema, not raw output and not one word. Long lossy handoffs mean a boundary through coupled work; a swelling window means a boundary that is too wide. Compaction for continuous work, notes for milestones, isolated sub-agents for independent branches.

days.title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Seven Domains

concepts.heading: Weights and Where to Spend the Last Hours
concepts.body: The exam has 45 scored questions in 90 minutes, and no pass mark is published. The domain weights are D1 Foundations of Context Engineering 16 percent, D2 System Prompt and Instruction Design 9, D3 Knowledge Retrieval and Genie Configuration 20, D4 Memory Architecture with Lakebase and MLflow 18, D5 Tool Design, MCP and Agent Context 13, D6 Context Compression and Compaction 11, and D7 Multi-Agent and Long-Horizon Task Design 13. Together D3 and D4 carry 38 percent, so review them first, then D1, then D5 and D7, and keep D6 and D2 for a last skim. Almost every item is a short scenario with a symptom and a decision; the wrong options are sensible fixes that cost recall, tokens or maintenance. So ask the same questions each time: what is in the window that should not be, what is missing that should be, and what is the smallest change that fixes it. Many terms are the exam guide's own convention, for example poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash, compaction and progressive disclosure, and the docs do not define them; do not look for a product setting behind them.

concepts.heading: D1 to D3: Foundations, Prompts and Retrieval
concepts.body: D1: match the failure to the technique. Poisoning is a wrong fact that persists, distraction is irrelevant material crowding out the task, confusion is too many look-alike or unnecessary tools, and clash is parts of the context that disagree. Prefer a minimal tool set, just-in-time retrieval and scoped tool results, because attention is a budget and long contexts degrade reasoning. For reasoning modes, weigh the thinking budget against the context it consumes. D2: prefer the targeted prompt revision with the lowest token and maintenance cost, keep few-shot examples only when their marginal contribution justifies the tokens, and judge a larger prompt with tracked experiment results. In Genie, curated example queries and trusted assets, column descriptions and filter expressions beat free text instructions, which are a last resort. D3: fix missing Unity Catalog metadata first, curate the right tables, views and functions into the space, and diagnose AI Search by configuration, chunking and the retrieval failure mode seen in eval logs. Limit retrieval to authoritative, governed sources. Choose pre-inference retrieval when the need is predictable and just-in-time retrieval when the agent must decide what to fetch.

concepts.heading: D4 to D6: Memory, Tools and Compaction
concepts.body: D4: match the memory type to the information need. Durable facts that must survive sessions belong in a Lakebase-backed store, scoped to the subject they describe, while exact task state belongs in a Delta-backed state object and not in an in-context scratchpad. Use structured queries for exact lookups and AI Search for fuzzy recall over text. Compare agent runs in MLflow 3 and pick the configuration that is reliably best, not the single best run. Retrieve dynamically when relevance varies, statically when it does not, and watch for over-retrieval that pollutes the window and under-retrieval that misses facts. Resolve intent before retrieval. D5: disclose tools progressively, write distinct tool descriptions, scope what tool results return, expose logic as Unity Catalog functions, and load Genie Code skills only when relevant. D6: notice the signs that compaction is due, then choose between summarising, clearing old tool results and trimming. Keep decisions, constraints and unresolved items; drop what can be fetched again. Every cut trades fidelity against cost and risk of losing a subtle detail.

concepts.heading: D7 and the Traps to Avoid
concepts.body: D7: diagnose missing shared context from conflicts and inconsistency, dispatch a compacted relevant trace slice rather than a bare task message, order dependent work and send conclusions with assumptions. Have sub-agents return a compact fixed schema, place boundaries where dependency is low, and match the long-horizon strategy to the work: compaction for continuous reasoning, notes for discrete milestones, isolated sub-agents for independent branches. These are the exam's convention and general practice, and MLflow Tracing, which records latency, token usage and cost per step, is the evidence for diagnosis. The traps repeat across domains. A bigger window is almost never the answer, because it delays the problem and keeps the noise. More text in the prompt is rarely right when a targeted change exists. Preview, Beta and Legacy features are not the stable choice, and the Genie multi-agent page is Public Preview. Lower temperature, a different model or an added review pass seldom fixes a missing-context cause. Finally, if a question names a constraint such as no larger window or lowest cost, the correct option must honour it.

examPoints: Weights: D1 16, D2 9, D3 20, D4 18, D5 13, D6 11, D7 13; D3 and D4 together are 38 percent, so they get the most review time.
Ask what should leave the window, what is missing, and what is the smallest fix that honours the stated constraint; a bigger window or more prompt text is rarely right.
Most context terms are the exam guide's convention, not Databricks features, and Preview features are never the answer and Beta or Legacy ones are not the stable choice.

quiz.q: An agent trace shows a long window full of old tool results from unrelated tasks, and accuracy falls over time. The team may not use a larger window or a Preview feature. Which first change matches the exam's reasoning?
choices: Raise the temperature so the model explores more of the history before it answers
Add a longer system prompt that tells the agent to ignore the old tool results
